claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and short telomeres are structurally similar, yet they have diametrically opposed fates.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and short telomeres are structurally similar, yet they have diametrically opposed fates.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that frames the biological problem being addressed.

claim: Cells must repair DSBs while blocking the action of telomerase on these ends.
source: Cells must repair DSBs while blocking the action of telomerase on these ends.
evidence: This is a statement of biological necessity based on established understanding of genome maintenance.

claim: Short telomeres must avoid recognition by the DNA damage response while promoting telomerase recruitment.
source: Short telomeres must avoid recognition by the DNA damage response while promoting telomerase recruitment.
evidence: This is a statement of biological necessity based on established understanding of telomere maintenance.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the Pif1 helicase is a telomerase inhibitor.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the Pif1 helicase, a telomerase inhibitor, lies at the interface of these end-fate decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by prior knowledge in the field.

claim: 34 bp of telomeric (TG1-3)n repeat sequence renders a DNA end insensitive to Pif1 action, thereby enabling extension by telomerase.
source: Using Pif1 as a sensor, we uncover a transition point in which 34 bp of telomeric (TG1-3)n repeat sequence renders a DNA end insensitive to Pif1 action, thereby enabling extension by telomerase.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A similar transition point exists at natural chromosome ends, where telomeres shorter than ~40 bp are inefficiently extended by telomerase.
source: A similar transition point exists at natural chromosome ends, where telomeres shorter than ~40 bp are inefficiently extended by telomerase.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by iSTEX assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The observed threshold of Pif1 activity defines a dividing line between DSBs and telomeres.
source: We contend that the observed threshold of Pif1 activity defines a dividing line between DSBs and telomeres.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: A failure to distinguish between DSBs and telomeres has severe consequences for genome integrity.
source: A failure to distinguish between these structures has severe consequences for genome integrity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: The engagement of the non-homologous end-joining pathway at telomeres can lead to breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that wreak havoc on the genome.
source: For example, the engagement of the non-homologous end-joining pathway at telomeres can lead to breakage-fusion-bridge cycles that wreak havoc on the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: The activity of telomerase at DSBs can generate new telomeres at the cost of the genetic information distal to the break.
source: Similarly, the activity of telomerase at DSBs can generate new telomeres at the cost of the genetic information distal to the break.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: Telomere addition has been observed in a variety of species.
source: Telomere addition has been observed in a variety of species (Kramer and Haber, 1993; Biessmann et al., 1990; Fouladi et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Telomere addition has been linked to human disorders involving terminal deletions of chromosome 16.
source: Telomere addition has been observed in a variety of species (Kramer and Haber, 1993; Biessmann et al., 1990; Fouladi et al., 2000) and has been linked to human disorders involving terminal deletions of chromosome 16 (Wilkie et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Telomere addition has been linked to human disorders involving terminal deletions of chromosome 22.
source: and has been linked to human disorders involving terminal deletions of chromosome 16 (Wilkie et al., 1990) and 22 (Wong et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae telomeres consist of 300 ± 75 bp of heterogeneous (TG1-3)n repeats.
source: The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose telomeres consist of 300 ± 75 bp of heterogeneous (TG1-3)n repeats, has been a key model to study mechanisms of genomic stability (Zakian, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: The telomere repeats organize a nucleoprotein structure minimally composed of the double-stranded (ds) DNA binding protein Rap1, its interacting factors Rif1 and Rif2, and the telomere-specific single-stranded (ss) DNA-binding Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complex.
source: The telomere repeats organize a nucleoprotein structure minimally composed of the double-stranded (ds) DNA binding protein Rap1, its interacting factors Rif1 and Rif2, and the telomere-specific single-stranded (ss) DNA-binding Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complex, which caps the chromosome ends (Dewar and Lydall, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Telomere-bound proteins prevent activation of DNA damage signaling pathways and the ability of the DSB repair machinery to use telomeric ends as substrates.
source: These telomere-bound proteins prevent activation of DNA damage signaling pathways and the ability of the DSB repair machinery to use telomeric ends as substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: The capping function is a universal property of eukaryotic telomeres.
source: This so-called capping function is a universal property of eukaryotic telomeres; while different in composition, a set of human proteins collectively known as shelterin accomplishes a similar function in human cells (Palm and de Lange, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Telomerase-mediated extension does not occur at every telomere in every cell cycle.
source: Telomerase-mediated extension does not occur at every telomere in every cell cycle, but the probability of telomere extension steadily increases as telomere length decreases (Teixeira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: The probability of telomere extension steadily increases as telomere length decreases.
source: Telomerase-mediated extension does not occur at every telomere in every cell cycle, but the probability of telomere extension steadily increases as telomere length decreases (Teixeira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Telomerase acts more processively at telomeres less than 125 bp in length, resulting in more extensive elongation of critically short telomeres.
source: Telomerase also acts more processively at telomeres less than 125 bp in length, resulting in more extensive elongation of critically short telomeres (Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Pif1 is a helicase that unwinds RNA-DNA hybrids in vitro and removes telomerase from telomeric DNA.
source: In addition, the telomerase inhibitor Pif1, which is a helicase that unwinds RNA-DNA hybrids in vitro and removes telomerase from telomeric DNA (Boulé et al., 2005), has recently been shown to act preferentially at long telomeres (Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations.

claim: Pif1 has recently been shown to act preferentially at long telomeres.
source: In addition, the telomerase inhibitor Pif1, which is a helicase that unwinds RNA-DNA hybrids in vitro and removes telomerase from telomeric DNA (Boulé et al., 2005), has recently been shown to act preferentially at long telomeres (Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Pif1 is required to inhibit telomerase at DSBs.
source: Remarkably, Pif1 is also required to inhibit telomerase at DSBs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge.

claim: Pif1 has both mitochondrial and nuclear isoforms encoded from separate translational start sites.
source: Pif1 has both mitochondrial and nuclear isoforms encoded from separate translational start sites; mutation of the second start site in the pif1-m2 mutant abolishes the nuclear isoform, resulting in telomere elongation (Schulz and Zakian, 1994) and a 240-fold increase in telomere addition at DSBs (Myung et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations.

claim: Mutation of the second start site in the pif1-m2 mutant abolishes the nuclear isoform, resulting in telomere elongation.
source: Pif1 has both mitochondrial and nuclear isoforms encoded from separate translational start sites; mutation of the second start site in the pif1-m2 mutant abolishes the nuclear isoform, resulting in telomere elongation (Schulz and Zakian, 1994) and a 240-fold increase in telomere addition at DSBs (Myung et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: The pif1-m2 mutant results in a 240-fold increase in telomere addition at DSBs.
source: Pif1 has both mitochondrial and nuclear isoforms encoded from separate translational start sites; mutation of the second start site in the pif1-m2 mutant abolishes the nuclear isoform, resulting in telomere elongation (Schulz and Zakian, 1994) and a 240-fold increase in telomere addition at DSBs (Myung et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: The Mec1 (ATR)-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc13 guards against the inappropriate recruitment of the CST complex to DSB sites.
source: The Mec1 (ATR)-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc13 also guards against the inappropriate recruitment of the CST complex to DSB sites (Zhang and Durocher, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Pif1 is able to distinguish between DSBs and telomeres.
source: One striking feature of Pif1 is that it is able to distinguish between DSBs and telomeres, as a pif1-4A mutant affects telomere addition frequency at DSBs but without influencing native telomere length (Makovets and Blackburn, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: A pif1-4A mutant affects telomere addition frequency at DSBs but without influencing native telomere length.
source: One striking feature of Pif1 is that it is able to distinguish between DSBs and telomeres, as a pif1-4A mutant affects telomere addition frequency at DSBs but without influencing native telomere length (Makovets and Blackburn, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation.

claim: Pif1 suppresses telomere addition at HO-induced DSBs containing 18 bp of (TG1-3)n telomeric repeats.
source: We noted in our previous work that Pif1 suppresses telomere addition at HO-induced DSBs containing 18 bp of (TG1-3)n telomeric repeats (referred to as TG18) but has no impact on the telomerase-dependent elongation of DNA ends containing a TG82 sequence (Zhang and Durocher, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pif1 has no impact on the telomerase-dependent elongation of DNA ends containing a TG82 sequence.
source: We noted in our previous work that Pif1 suppresses telomere addition at HO-induced DSBs containing 18 bp of (TG1-3)n telomeric repeats (referred to as TG18) but has no impact on the telomerase-dependent elongation of DNA ends containing a TG82 sequence (Zhang and Durocher, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The TG82 substrate behaves as a critically short telomere and cells elongate it in a manner that is uninhibited by Pif1.
source: This observation suggests that the TG82 substrate behaves as a critically short telomere and that cells elongate it in a manner that is uninhibited by Pif1.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the introduction based on prior observations.

claim: Similar rates of telomere addition were observed at all DNA ends containing 34, 45, 56, and 67 bp of telomeric repeats in both wild-type and pif1-m2 backgrounds.
source: We observed similar rates of telomere addition at all DNA ends in both backgrounds, indicating that 34 bp of telomeric repeats are sufficient to render a DNA end insensitive to Pif1 (Figure 1c; source data are available in Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 34 bp of telomeric repeats are sufficient to render a DNA end insensitive to Pif1.
source: We observed similar rates of telomere addition at all DNA ends in both backgrounds, indicating that 34 bp of telomeric repeats are sufficient to render a DNA end insensitive to Pif1 (Figure 1c; source data are available in Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Analysis of DNA ends by Southern blot revealed robust telomere addition at the TG34 substrate in PIF1 cells.
source: Analysis of DNA ends by Southern blot also revealed robust telomere addition at the TG34 substrate in PIF1 cells, mirroring the results of the genetic assay (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Asynchronously dividing cells exhibited a similar phenotype at the TG18 and TG34 ends as nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: However, asynchronously dividing cells also exhibited a similar phenotype at the TG18 and TG34 ends (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b; source data are available in Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The addition of RAD52 reduced telomere addition at the TG18 end in pif1-m2 cells but had no impact on the behavior of Pif1 at the TG34 substrate.
source: The addition of RAD52 in this assay reduced telomere addition at the TG18 end in pif1-m2 cells but had no impact on the behavior of Pif1 at the TG34 substrate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Pif1 is active at DNA ends up to TG26, while the frequency of telomere addition increased at the TG30 end and beyond.
source: Analysis of telomere addition revealed that Pif1 is active at DNA ends up to TG26, while the frequency of telomere addition increased at the TG30 end and beyond (Figure 1e; source data are available in Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Telomere addition was inhibited by Pif1 at all TG26 ends, while the corresponding TG36 ends resulted in telomere addition in the presence of Pif1.
source: Consistent with our initial observations, telomere addition was inhibited by Pif1 at all TG26 ends, while the corresponding TG36 ends resulted in telomere addition in the presence of Pif1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d; source data for panel c are available in Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d.

claim: The 26 to 34 bp window of telomeric sequence is the dividing line between what the cell interprets to be a DSB and what is considered to be a critically short telomere.
source: By using Pif1-insensitivity as an operational definition of a short telomere, we propose that the 26 to 34 bp window of telomeric sequence is the dividing line between what the cell interprets to be a DSB and what is considered to be a critically short telomere.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 1.

claim: DNA ends containing 34 bp or more of telomeric DNA are allowed to elongate in a manner unimpeded by Pif1.
source: These data suggest that DNA ends containing 34 bp or more of telomeric DNA are allowed to elongate in a manner unimpeded by Pif1 and we herein refer to this phenomenon as the DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: At the V-R telomere, only two out of 32 telomeres (6.3%) shorter than 44 bp were extended by telomerase, while 65 out of 136 telomeres (47.8%) between 44 bp and 86 bp long were extended.
source: At the V-R telomere, only two out of 32 telomeres (6.3%) shorter than 44 bp were extended by telomerase, while 65 out of 136 telomeres (47.8%) between 44 bp and 86 bp long were extended.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: At the VI-R telomere, two of the 13 telomeres below 38 bp (15.4%) were extended, while 51 out of 115 telomeres (44.3%) between 38 bp and 74 bp long were extended.
source: Similarly, at the VI-R telomere, two of the 13 telomeres below 38 bp (15.4%) were extended, while 51 out of 115 telomeres (44.3%) between 38 bp and 74 bp long were extended.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: While telomerase preferentially elongates short telomeres, those below ~40 bp are inefficiently extended.
source: Thus, while telomerase preferentially elongates short telomeres, those below ~40 bp are inefficiently extended.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the iSTEX assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The DSB-telomere transition identified at HO-induced breaks also exists at native chromosome ends.
source: These data suggest that the DSB-telomere transition identified at HO-induced breaks also exists at native chromosome ends.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the iSTEX assay data.

claim: At both the V-R and VI-R telomeres, the percentage of elongated telomeres below the DSB-telomere transition length determined in PIF1 cells increased in the pif1-m2 background.
source: At both the V-R and VI-R telomeres, the percentage of elongated telomeres below the DSB-telomere transition length determined in PIF1 cells increased in the pif1-m2 background (although statistical significance was not reached for the VI-R telomere due to difficulties in obtaining enough short telomeres for analysis).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: At both DSBs and chromosome ends, Pif1 is needed to set the DSB-telomere transition.
source: Thus, at both DSBs and chromosome ends, Pif1 is needed to set the DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the iSTEX assay data in pif1-m2 cells.

claim: Although telomere addition was reduced in tel1Δ cells, a similar reduction was observed in tel1Δ pif1-m2 cells, indicating that TEL1 and PIF1 function in separate pathways.
source: Although telomere addition was reduced in tel1Δ cells, we observed a similar reduction in tel1Δ pif1-m2 cells, indicating that TEL1 and PIF1 function in separate pathways (Figure 3a,b; source data for panel b are available in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: The loss of TEL1 did not affect the DSB-telomere transition at the TG18 and TG34 DNA ends.
source: Consistent with this observation, the loss of TEL1 did not affect the DSB-telomere transition at the TG18 and TG34 DNA ends (Figure 3c; source data are available in Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Loss of MEC1 and RAD53 failed to inhibit telomerase in a Pif1-specific manner at the TG82 end.
source: Loss of MEC1 and RAD53 also failed to inhibit telomerase in a Pif1-specific manner at the TG82 end (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d; source data are available in Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1, 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d.

claim: Mutation of five consensus S/T-Q Mec1 and Tel1 phosphorylation sites in the pif1-5AQ allele did not decrease telomere addition at the TG34 end.
source: Pif1 contains five consensus S/T-Q Mec1 and Tel1 phosphorylation sites; however, their mutation in the pif1-5AQ allele (S148A/S180A/T206A/S707A/T811A) also did not decrease telomere addition at the TG34 end (Figure 3d; source data are available in Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Expression of Cdc13-Est1 and Cdc13-Est2 fusion proteins resulted in greatly elongated telomeres.
source: In agreement with previous work, expression of both fusions resulted in greatly elongated telomeres (Evans and Lundblad, 1999) (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4a and a citation to prior work.

claim: Cdc13-Est1 and Cdc13-Est2 fusion proteins did not increase telomere addition at the TG18 DNA end in the presence of Pif1.
source: In agreement with previous work, expression of both fusions resulted in greatly elongated telomeres (Evans and Lundblad, 1999) (Figure 4a); however, they did not increase telomere addition at the TG18 DNA end in the presence of Pif1 (Figure 4b; source data are available in Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Cdc13-Est1K444E can extend the TG18 end only in the absence of PIF1.
source: We observed that Cdc13-Est1K444E can extend the TG18 end only in the absence of PIF1 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Pif1 is able to effectively suppress telomere addition even in the presence of enhanced telomerase recruitment.
source: Together, these data indicate that Pif1 is able to effectively suppress telomere addition even in the presence of enhanced telomerase recruitment, suggesting that increased telomerase recruitment to the TG34 end is unlikely to underpin the observed DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Cdc13-Est1/Est2 fusion experiments.

claim: The pif1-4D mutant did not restore Pif1 activity at the TG34 DNA end.
source: Contrary to this prediction, the pif1-4D mutant did not restore Pif1 activity at the TG34 DNA end (Figure 4c), indicating that phosphorylation of these sites is not sufficient to regulate the DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Phosphorylation of T763/S765/S766/S769 sites is not sufficient to regulate the DSB-telomere transition.
source: Contrary to this prediction, the pif1-4D mutant did not restore Pif1 activity at the TG34 DNA end (Figure 4c), indicating that phosphorylation of these sites is not sufficient to regulate the DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pif1-4D mutant data.

claim: The pif1-4A mutation affects the frequency of telomere addition at DSBs, but does not affect native telomere length.
source: First, the pif1-4A mutation affects the frequency of telomere addition at DSBs, but does not affect native telomere length (Makovets and Blackburn, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by a citation.

claim: The inability of the pif1-4D allele to inhibit telomerase at TG34 provides indirect evidence that the cell interprets this DNA end as a short telomere.
source: The inability of the pif1-4D allele to inhibit telomerase at TG34 therefore provides indirect evidence that the cell interprets this DNA end as a short telomere.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pif1-4D mutant data.

claim: The est2-up34 mutant results in over-elongated telomeres in wild-type but not pif1-m2 cells.
source: Interestingly, the est2-up34 mutant results in over-elongated telomeres in wild-type but not pif1-m2 cells, indicating that the est2-up34 allele can at least partially bypass Pif1 inhibition (Eugster et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by a citation.

claim: Although increased telomere length was observed in PIF1 est2-up34 cells, telomere addition was not increased, indicating that the est2-up34 mutation can bypass Pif1 function at telomeres but not at DSBs.
source: Although we observed increased telomere length in PIF1 est2-up34 cells (Figure 4d), telomere addition was not increased (Figure 4e; source data are available in Figure 4—source data 3), indicating that the est2-up34 mutation can bypass Pif1 function at telomeres but not at DSBs.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 4d,e.

claim: Pif1 possesses distinct functions at DSBs and telomeres and these differences are recapitulated in the TG18 and TG34 DNA ends on either side of the DSB-telomere transition.
source: Together these data support the idea that Pif1 possesses distinct functions at DSBs and telomeres and that these differences are recapitulated in the TG18 and TG34 DNA ends on either side of the DSB-telomere transition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pif1-4A and est2-up34 mutant data.

claim: The loss of either the MRX or Ku complex did not affect either side of the DSB-telomere transition.
source: The loss of either complex, however, did not affect either side of the DSB-telomere transition (Figure 5a; source data are available in Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Increased telomere addition was observed at TG36 ends in wild-type cells despite the use of synthetic telomeric sequences lacking a CCC motif.
source: Despite these alterations, we still observed increased telomere addition at TG36 ends in wild-type cells (Figure 5b; source data are available in Figure 5—source data 2), suggesting that Rap1 binding is not required for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Rap1 binding is not required for the DSB-telomere transition.
source: Despite these alterations, we still observed increased telomere addition at TG36 ends in wild-type cells (Figure 5b; source data are available in Figure 5—source data 2), suggesting that Rap1 binding is not required for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the synthetic telomeric sequence experiments.

claim: Telomere addition at the TG34 end was unaltered in rif1Δ rif2Δ mutants.
source: Consistent with a Rap1-independent mechanism, telomere addition at the TG34 end was unaltered in rif1Δ rif2Δ mutants (Figure 5c; source data are available in Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The Cdc13 N-terminal OB-fold domain (OB1) forms dimers.
source: The Cdc13 N-terminal OB-fold domain (OB1) (Figure 6a) forms dimers (Mitchell et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by citations.

claim: Telomere addition at the TG34 end was inhibited by Pif1 in cdc13-L91A cells.
source: Consistent with this prediction, telomere addition at the TG34 end was inhibited by Pif1 in cdc13-L91A cells (Figure 6b; source data are available in Figure 6—source data 1)
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: cdc13-L91A mutants exhibited a growth defect that was suppressed by pif1-m2.
source: however, further investigation revealed a growth defect in these mutants that was suppressed by pif1-m2 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: High copy plasmid expression of cdc13-L91A was able to rescue the growth defect, but also increased telomere addition at the TG34 substrate.
source: High copy plasmid expression of cdc13-L91A was able to rescue the growth defect, but also increased telomere addition at the TG34 substrate (Figure 6b)
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Screening of approximately 6000 mutants led to the identification of fifteen hits that exhibited impaired telomere addition at the TG34 substrate.
source: Screening of approximately 6000 mutants led to the identification of fifteen hits that exhibited impaired telomere addition at the TG34 substrate.
evidence: This is a finding from the CDC13 mutagenesis screen.

claim: Eight clones were identified in which telomere addition was impaired in wild-type cells but relatively unaffected in pif1-m2 cells.
source: and eight clones in which telomere addition was impaired in wild-type cells but relatively unaffected in pif1-m2 cells (#1, 2, 3, 42, 63, 71, 72, and 77) (Figure 6f; source data are available in Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the CDC13 mutagenesis screen supported by data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The third group of Cdc13 mutations specifically sensitize the TG34 end to the activity of Pif1.
source: This observation suggested that the third group of Cdc13 mutations specifically sensitize the TG34 end to the activity of Pif1 and are herein referred to as cdc13-sp alleles (sensitive to Pif1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CDC13 mutagenesis screen results.

claim: Three alleles had contributions from multiple substitutions: I87N and Y758N in cdc13-sp1, H12R and F728I in cdc13-sp72, and E566V, N567D, and Q583K in cdc13-sp3.
source: Three alleles had contributions from multiple substitutions: I87N and Y758N in cdc13-sp1, H12R and F728I in cdc13-sp72, and E566V, N567D, and Q583K in cdc13-sp3 (Figure 7a; source data are available in Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from mapping experiments supported by data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The most important mutation in cdc13-sp3 was identified to be Q583K with a minor contribution from E556V/N567D.
source: The most important mutation in cdc13-sp3 was identified to be Q583K with a minor contribution from E556V/N567D.
evidence: This is a finding from mapping experiments.

claim: All three residues (E566, N567, Q583) are found in the canonical DNA-binding domain.
source: Interestingly, all three residues are found in the canonical DNA-binding domain, suggesting that weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomeric DNA can also sensitize the TG34 end to Pif1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is based on structural knowledge.

claim: Weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomeric DNA can sensitize the TG34 end to Pif1.
source: Interestingly, all three residues are found in the canonical DNA-binding domain, suggesting that weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomeric DNA can also sensitize the TG34 end to Pif1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the location of the mutations.

claim: Three single amino acid residues (F236, S255, Q256) could completely account for the phenotype of cdc13-sp63, cdc13-sp42, and cdc13-sp77, respectively.
source: Three single amino acid residues (F236, S255, Q256) could completely account for the phenotype of the remaining three alleles (cdc13-sp63, cdc13-sp42, and cdc13-sp77, respectively; Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from mapping experiments supported by data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: F236, S255, and Q256 all map to the Cdc13 telomerase recruitment domain.
source: These residues all map to the Cdc13 telomerase recruitment domain, suggesting that weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomerase is another means to facilitate Pif1 activity at TG34.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is based on structural knowledge.

claim: Weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomerase is another means to facilitate Pif1 activity at TG34.
source: These residues all map to the Cdc13 telomerase recruitment domain, suggesting that weakening the association of Cdc13 with telomerase is another means to facilitate Pif1 activity at TG34.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the location of the mutations.

claim: The S255A mutation has previously been shown to impair telomerase recruitment, resulting in telomere shortening.
source: In particular, the S255A mutation has previously been shown to impair telomerase recruitment, resulting in telomere shortening (Gao et al., 2010; Tseng et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and is supported by citations.

claim: The classic telomerase null cdc13-2 (E252K) mutant was also sensitive to Pif1.
source: Similarly, the classic telomerase null cdc13-2 (E252K) mutant (Nugent et al., 1996) was also sensitive to Pif1 (Figure 7b; source data are available in Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The cdc13-1 mutant grown at permissive temperature was also sensitive to Pif1.
source: In agreement with this idea, the cdc13-1 mutant grown at permissive temperature was also sensitive to Pif1, (Figure 7b)
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7b.
